title: The Maures range, schists and quartzites: why the gulf landscapes take this shape
author: Caramagnols
excerpt: The Gulf of Saint-Tropez is not explained by the sea alone. Its villages, slopes, short valleys and vegetation also depend on the older geology of the Maures range.
content:
The gulf is often reduced to harbours and beaches. Yet as soon as one gains a little height or moves away from the shore, the Maures range imposes its structure. It gives the territory its breaks in slope, lean soils, short valleys and part of its botany.

An old relief still present behind the seaside image

The Maures bedrock rests largely on schists, gneisses and quartzites. That base produces a firmer relief than one imagines from the quays alone: short slopes, ridges, tighter valleys and quick transitions between plain and height.

Soils that govern woodland, vines and paths

The nature of the soils explains much in the siting of villages and crops. Cork oaks, pines, scrubland, vineyards and dry-stone walls are not scattered at random; they answer to rock, exposure, available water and the proximity of the sea.

Another way of reading the gulf

Once this geology is understood, the walk changes. It becomes easier to see why some villages stay perched, why others spread towards the plain, why roads turn so much and why light feels harsher in some sectors than in others.

This note extends the page Walking Around the Gulf of Saint-Tropez. To continue within the same cluster, it also helps to open When to visit the Gulf of Saint-Tropez: out of season, morning, late day or summer?.
